newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia monarchy crisis deepens coalition rift.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia monarchy crisis deepens coalition rift.

text.p: A monarchy crisis in Cambodia has widened cracks in the nation's fragile coalition government while raising fears of a new phase of political feuding, diplomats and analysts said.

The monarchy, once a stabilising force in Cambodian politics, is now at the centre of a growing confrontation between co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen ahead of local and national elections, scheduled for 1997 and 1998.

The two leaders, whose parties will face each other in the polls, are locked in what diplomats describe as one of the most divisive disputes to hit the coalition since it was installed after U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993.

Some say the coalition is failing, a scenario which the international community considers particularly disheartening given the country's history of feuding leaders and the great effort and costs related to the 1993 elections.
Those polls were a $2 billion drain on international aid for a country also faced with widespread poverty, backward infrastructure and deep scars from years of civil war.
"We're all fed up. It's hard to take the political process here too seriously...and living under the pressure of it gets really old," said one international aid worker.
Upcoming elections, combined with King Norodom Sihanouk's comment last month that he was contemplating abdication, apparently triggered the latest troubles.

Hun Sen and his backers fear the possibility of Sihanouk abdicating and using his enormous popularity to propel Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party and its allies to victory in the polls, analysts said.
Sihanouk, 74, abdicated to enter politics in 1995 after 14 years on the throne, but he said this time he had no intention to pursue politics.
Hun Sen has vowed to cancel elections if the king abdicated to enter politics, and plans to ask Sihanouk to ban royal family members from politics unless they renounced their royal status.

Ranariddh has reacted by adopting a tough pro-royalist stance at FUNCINPEC's recent party congress, calling for the return of two exiled princes despised by Hun Sen and expressing support for the king if he entered politics.

Ranariddh has also said he would file a complaint against Hun Sen with the U.N. Commission on Human Rights in Geneva, which observers say appears linked to Hun Sen's recent attacks on the monarchy. However he has yet to do so.
Sihanouk, meanwhile, remains in Beijing for medical treatment while Cambodians wonder whether he will return to make peace, surrender the throne or become a political player.
Those close to Sihanouk said that even if he does harbour some political ambitions, he may not act on them given the current bitter political environment.
"He's not fulfilling the (peacemaker) role he can play...it may be he is so frustrated (with the infighting), he doesn't really want to go on. He is really very sad," said one observer.
He is not the only one tired of the political brawls which have spanned issues such as power-sharing and the recent defection of some senior Khmer Rouge guerrillas.

Moderates such as the Deputy Prime Minister Sar Kheng, who belongs to Hun Sen's ex-communist Cambodia's People's Party (CPP), have made recent appeals for calm and urged political leaders to put national interest first.
Donors -- whose aid accounts for half of Cambodia's national budget -- say they are beginning to feel less generous.

"I see compassion fatigue and I don't blame the (donors)," said Kassie Neou of the Cambodian Institute of Human Rights. "Cambodia should not sit back with outstretched hands and keep asking. No one will keep giving if they don't see progress."

But he added that Cambodia's problems are now also the problems of the international community because of the massive aid it has injected into the country. "Cambodia's failures will become the failures of the international community," he warned.
